tier_reason: The README Benchmark section shows the author's own ApacheBench runs against nginx/1.14.0 (worker_processes 1) with every quoted number present (123907.91 vs 74441.26 req/s keep-alive, 27605.45 vs 15773.47 req/s Connection: close), but no compiler, flags, CPU model or benchmark server source/build target is given, so first-party with partial methodology: C.

corrections.caveats: The author states the run was only a micro-benchmark for a performance reference point and explicitly makes no statement of superiority, since httpserver.h is not a competitor or replacement for NGINX. Compiler, flags and CPU model are not stated, and the repo has no benchmark target (the Makefile only builds Debug tests and a -O0 fuzzer), so the exact server binary and build are unknown. The numbers date from the README's first commits (2019-12-12) and were never re-run; the library has since been restructured (src/ split, m4-generated single header, 2026 socket-leak fixes). The nginx config shown is minimal (worker_processes 1, a return 200 location) and does not disable access logging; nginx also sent more bytes per response (about 210 vs 134 keep-alive and 205 vs 129 close, derived from page data) because of its headers. In the keep-alive run nginx served 99,052 of 100,000 requests as keep-alive (consistent with nginx's default keepalive_requests 100 forcing reconnects) and had 1 s connect outliers (max 1150 ms), so the keep-alive gap partly reflects nginx defaults. Hello-world workload with ab as a single-threaded client on localhost, nginx version from 2018 (1.14.0). Own benchmark with partial methodology, so tier C.

notes: Numbers, baseline, MIT license, 1.9k stars, last commit 2026-04-26 (active) all verified. Shortcomings: 2019 numbers on an older code version, no compiler/flags/CPU, no benchmark build target in repo, nginx left at default access logging and keepalive_requests, author disclaims any superiority claim.

tier_reason: The quoted numbers are on benchmarks/README.md, but the pure Boost.Beast baseline (benchmarks/beast_benchmark/boost_beast_benchmark.cpp) calls socket_.shutdown(shutdown_send) and accept() (which closes the socket) after every response, so wrk reconnects for every baseline request (read errors equal the request count in all three runs) while Ichor keeps connections alive; the measured win is a harness artifact, leaving no valid number showing Ichor faster than Beast (crippled-baseline precedent, as with AssemblyScript C to D).

corrections.claimed_speedup: No valid like-for-like win. Page rows, Ichor + Boost.Beast (keep-alive, 60 s runs) vs a pure Boost.Beast server that closes the connection after every response (10 s runs): 67,194.72 vs 41,397.00 req/s at 2 connections (about 1.6x, derived from page data), 87,048.80 vs 73,975.13 at 400 (about 1.18x, derived from page data), 72,971.55 vs 37,311.37 at 20,000 (about 1.96x, derived from page data). At 2 connections the Beast baseline's mean latency is lower (20.80 us vs 29.17 us), so its lower throughput comes from per-request reconnects. Drogon (132,285.77 / 132,936.53 / 117,676.17 req/s) and Go fasthttp (165,747.41 / 170,028.45 / 123,741.19 req/s) are faster than Ichor on the same page.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Ichor built with cmake -GNinja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DICHOR_ARCH_OPTIMIZATION=X86_64_AVX2 -DICHOR_USE_BOOST_BEAST=ON -DICHOR_USE_SANITIZERS=OFF; the README setup line lists gcc 13.1.1 and clang 18 but does not say which compiled the HTTP runs. The Beast baseline is compiled in the same tree (guarded by ICHOR_USE_BOOST_BEAST); its num_workers and spin/block arguments for the runs are not stated.
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers, and the comparison is invalid as a speed claim: the pure Beast baseline in benchmarks/beast_benchmark/boost_beast_benchmark.cpp (adapted from Beast's http_server_fast example) sets keep_alive(true) in the response but then shuts down the send side and closes the socket after every response, so wrk must open a new TCP connection per request (every baseline run shows read errors equal to its request count: 418,099 / 740,671 / 374,703), while Ichor's pong example keeps connections alive and shows no socket errors. At 2 connections Beast's mean latency (20.80 us) is lower than Ichor's (29.17 us). Ichor is itself layered on Boost.Beast, and its README goal is only 'performance matching at least Boost Beast'. Ichor runs lasted 60 s and Beast runs 10 s; the Beast worker count is not stated. The benchmarks README says the benchmarks identify bottlenecks and do not showcase performance; proper throughput and latency benchmarks are TBD. The file was last updated 2024-02-02. Drogon and Go fasthttp are about 1.5x to 2.5x faster than Ichor on the same page. Hardware (AMD 7950X) is stated only at the top of the README for the preliminary core benchmarks.

notes: Downgrade C to D: baseline Beast server closes every connection (shutdown_send + close after each response; wrk read errors = request count), Ichor uses keep-alive, so the 1.18x-1.96x figures are a harness artifact; with the lower Beast latency at 2 connections there is no valid evidence Ichor is faster than Beast. MIT, 237 stars, last commit 2026-02-06 (active) verified; keep-and-document candidate, not a fabrication.
